city.authors: Geoff Pike and Jyrki Alakuijala · Google
city.background: CityHash is a family of fast string hashes developed at Google. It is designed for uses such as hash tables, where a string needs to be turned into a small integer quickly. This entry studies the 64-bit function that accepts a seed.

farm.background: FarmHash is Google’s successor to CityHash. It offers several implementations tuned for different processors. The chart uses the 64-bit NA implementation, so this entry should not be read as a result about every FarmHash variant.

murmur.background: MurmurHash3 is Austin Appleby’s widely used non-cryptographic hash family. Appleby also created SMHasher, the testing tool discussed in this post. The x64_128 variant is built for 64-bit processors and returns a 128-bit result.

mx3.background: mx3 combines a small integer mixer, a random-number generator and a string hash. Its hash uses ordinary multiplication and bit operations, making the implementation compact. The version studied here is v3.

fasthash-64.background: Fasthash is a compact C hash by Zilong Tan. It processes eight bytes at a time with multiplication and bit mixing. The 32-bit function is derived from the same computation as the 64-bit function.

muse.background: MuseAir is a portable hash built around multiplication of large integers. This entry concerns the historical v0.3 implementation retained in SMHasher3. Later releases are different algorithms and need separate analysis.

komi.background: Komihash is a fast 64-bit hash supplied as a C/C++ header. It splits work among several parallel calculations to improve speed. This result concerns versions 5.27 and 5.34 and messages of 64–127 bytes.

t1ha.background: t1ha, short for Fast Positive Hash, is a family designed for fast hashing on ordinary processors. This entry studies t1ha2’s one-shot 64-bit function, which hashes a complete message in a single call.

a5.background: a5hash is a C/C++ hash-table hash from the author of komihash. Version 5.21 offers both 64-bit and 128-bit outputs. The two output sizes have different collision results here.

rapid3.authors: Nicolas De Carli · based on wyhash by Wang Yi
rapid3.background: Rapidhash develops ideas from Wang Yi’s wyhash, using multiplication to mix message data quickly. Version 3 offers standard, Micro and Nano variants with different speed and code-size tradeoffs. The chart studies the standard variant.

mum.background: MUM stands for “multiply and mix”: it combines the two halves of a large integer product. This entry uses the historical v3 implementation and constants studied in the post. Later collision-prevention changes are outside this result.

mir.background: This hash comes from Vladimir Makarov’s MIR compiler project. It mixes data by adding the two halves of a large product. The “exact” and “inexact” implementations use different ways to compute that product; the chart times the exact one.

xxh3-64.authors: Yann Collet and the xxHash contributors
xxh3-64.background: XXH3 is part of Yann Collet’s xxHash family. It uses different routines for different input lengths and processors to achieve high throughput. These entries study version 0.8.3’s seeded functions with the standard public constants.

highway.authors: Jyrki Alakuijala, Bill Cox, and Jan Wassenberg · Google
highway.background: HighwayHash was designed at Google as a fast keyed hash. It uses processor instructions that work on several values at once and offers 64-, 128- and 256-bit outputs. Its key contains four 64-bit words.

spooky.background: SpookyHash is Bob Jenkins’s non-cryptographic hash for 64-bit machines. It computes a 128-bit result and also offers a 64-bit interface. The chart studies that 64-bit interface in version 2.

pengyhash.background: Pengyhash is a compact hash built from additions, rotations and bit operations. Version 0.3 returns 64 bits and accepts a 64-bit seed. Earlier versions used a smaller seed.

nmhash32.background: NMHASH32 and NMHASH32X are two distinct 32-bit hashes by James Z. M. Gao. Both accept a 32-bit seed, but use different mixing routines. Each therefore needs its own collision analysis.

gx.background: GxHash is a fast hash implemented in Rust that uses the processor’s AES instructions to mix data. This entry studies version 3.5.0. Using AES instructions inside a hash does not, by itself, establish a collision guarantee.

ahash.background: aHash is a Rust hash designed for hash tables. It uses AES hardware instructions when they are available and a different fallback otherwise. This entry concerns the AES implementation in version 0.8.12.

polymur.background: PolymurHash is Orson Peters’s fast hash with a mathematical collision guarantee. It treats a message as a polynomial—a sum of powers with the message pieces as coefficients—and evaluates it using a secret key. It uses ordinary integer multiplication, so it does not require specialized carry-less multiplication instructions.

halftimehash-64.background: HalftimeHash, introduced by Jim Apple in 2021, was designed to hash long strings quickly without relying on wide integer multiplication. Its 64, 128, 256 and 512 style names describe implementation choices: every style here returns a 64-bit hash.

umash.background: UMASH was developed at Backtrace to give fast string fingerprints with a mathematical bound on accidental matches. It combines several hashing steps. The 128-bit fingerprint adds a second result to the 64-bit hash.

clhash.background: CLHASH is a fast universal hash designed by Daniel Lemire and Owen Kaser. It uses specialized processor instructions for a form of binary multiplication. The design aims to combine a collision guarantee with high throughput on long messages.

chain256.authors: Thomas Dybdahl Ahle · author of this post
chain256.background: ChainHash is my construction for hashing long messages with a provable collision bound. This version processes 256-byte blocks and combines their results with secret-key arithmetic. It is the original design from the paper, retained in Table 2; v3 is now the shipped default and the 64-bit ChainHash point on both hosts.

poly1305.background: Poly1305 is the polynomial-hashing component of Daniel J. Bernstein’s message-authentication design. It helps detect whether a message has been altered. The chart compares that mathematical component and an OpenSSL implementation; using it as a complete authenticator requires the surrounding protocol.

ghash.authors: David A. McGrew and John Viega · GCM construction
ghash.background: GHASH is the polynomial hash inside GCM, an authenticated-encryption design by David McGrew and John Viega. In systems such as AES-GCM it helps detect changes to data. Here it provides a useful comparison with the faster general-purpose hashes.

foldhash-fast.background: Foldhash is Orson Peters’s Rust hash for hash tables. It mixes data using large integer products. Version 0.2.0 has a fast variant and a quality variant that adds another mixing step.

siphash-1-3.authors: Jean-Philippe Aumasson and Daniel J. Bernstein
siphash-1-3.background: SipHash was designed by Jean-Philippe Aumasson and Daniel J. Bernstein for keyed hashing, including protection against hash-table flooding. The 1-3 and 2-4 variants use different numbers of mixing rounds, trading speed for a larger security margin. Both variants are plotted here as claims at the 64-bit output width.

halftime24.background: HalftimeHash’s advanced interface can return 24 bytes, or 192 bits, rather than the 64 bits returned by its public wrappers. This entry studies that original internal function. It was intended for fixed-length inputs.

halftime24-fixed.authors: Jim Apple; repairs by Thomas Dybdahl Ahle
halftime24-fixed.background: This is a repaired version of HalftimeHash’s advanced 24-byte function. It changes how message blocks are encoded and records the input length explicitly. The repair is studied in the linked branch; it is not presented as an upstream HalftimeHash release. Not plotted: the post repairs the proof, and the encoder only to check it; it does not ship fixed hashes.

chain-v2.authors: Thomas Dybdahl Ahle · author of this post
chain-v2.background: ChainHash v2 rearranges my original ChainHash design to process neighboring pieces of data together in 1,024-byte blocks. This layout targets faster processing on x86 processors. It produces different hash values from the original paper version.

chain128.authors: Thomas Dybdahl Ahle · author of this post
chain128.background: ChainHash-128 is the 128-bit version of my ChainHash construction. It processes messages in 512-byte blocks and combines them using secret-key arithmetic. Its wider output makes room for a stronger collision guarantee than the 64-bit versions.

go-maphash.background: Go uses its runtime hash for string map keys and exposes the byte-sequence hash through hash/maphash. The implementation selects a processor-specific path; this entry studies go1.27.1 on amd64 with AES instructions.

abseil-hash.background: Abseil supplies C++ hash functions and SwissTable containers such as flat_hash_map. absl::Hash aims to mix ordinary inputs well and vary results between processes. Its source explicitly says the process seed is not a security feature.

dotnet-marvin.background: Marvin is the small add–rotate–xor hash used by .NET for string hash codes. It starts from a random 64-bit seed and returns 32 bits. This entry studies the .NET 10 string path, which hashes UTF-16 bytes.

chain-v3.authors: Thomas Dybdahl Ahle · author of this post
chain-v3.background: ChainHash v3 (ChainHash-Horner) is my default construction for hashing long messages with a collision guarantee. It combines 256-byte logical blocks with a secret-key polynomial. Its flat product loop follows Orson Peters’s PolymurHash design lineage. The public repository ships chainhash3.h alongside the original paper function, chainhash.h; v3 changes the digests.

muse-v2.background: MuseAir is a multiply-based non-cryptographic hash. Algorithm v2, released as crate 0.6.0, mixes the seed into tail products and supersedes the deprecated earlier algorithms. Its README warns against direct server use with its single-seed interface.

rows.name: CityHash64 v1.1.1
rows.label: CityHash64
rows.scope: Exact sufficient contribution; other pairs or collision events may lower the score.
rows.key_model: Uniform 64-bit WithSeed seed; structural result also holds for all pairs of 64-bit seeds.
rows.summary: Two different eight-byte messages already have the same intermediate result before the seed is mixed in. From that point onward, the computation is identical. The pair therefore collides for every seed, so keeping the seed secret or replacing it does not help.

reader_notes.evidence: The algebra shows that this pair collides for every seed. Trying a new seed cannot separate these two messages.
reader_notes.key: The experiment chooses a 64-bit seed at random, with every possible value equally likely. The two messages are chosen first and do not depend on that seed.
reader_notes.scope: The result covers the studied CityHash64 seeded functions, including the version that accepts two seeds. It extends earlier published attacks; the appendix credits that work and gives the exact inputs.

rows.name: MurmurHash3 x64_128
rows.label: MurmurHash3 x64_128
rows.scope: Exact sufficient contribution; other pairs or collision events may lower the score.
rows.key_model: Uniform 32-bit API seed (SMHasher3 truncates seed_t to uint32_t at hashes/murmurhash3.cpp lines 227-228; the reference API takes uint32_t); all 2^32 seeds enumerated and re-enumerated 2026-09-18 against upstream HEAD.
rows.summary: A carefully chosen change in one part of the message can be cancelled by a later change. Both halves of the 128-bit result then agree for every seed. The wider output does not protect against two messages that reach the same internal state.

reader_notes.evidence: The argument is algebraic, and the supplied verification also checks every possible 32-bit seed.
reader_notes.key: The public function accepts a 32-bit seed. Each of its roughly 4.3 billion possible values is equally likely in the stated experiment.
reader_notes.scope: The result concerns MurmurHash3 x64_128. It builds on a previously published method; the appendix explains the extension and credits the original work.

rows.name: mx3 v3
rows.label: mx3 v3
rows.scope: Exact sufficient contribution; other pairs or collision events may lower the score. This is mx3 v3.0.0, tag 48924ee7, with a 64-bit seed. rurban’s mx3 entry tests v1.0.0 (0x4DB51E5B) with a 32-bit seed cast to 64 bits; its GOOD label and older bad-seed result do not describe the attacked v3.
rows.key_model: 64 (`inline uint64_t hash(const uint8_t* buf, size_t len, uint64_t seed)`; v3 seeds via h = mix_stream(seed, len + 1), v1/v2 via h = seed ^ len). The seed enters only through the additive term C^(L+1)*seed of the pre-finalizer state, before a public bijective finalizer mix(). SMHasher3: 64.
rows.summary: One one-byte message and one eight-byte message are chosen so that their contents cancel the difference in their lengths. They reach the same state before the final mixing step and collide for every seed.

reader_notes.evidence: The algebra shows that this pair collides for every seed. Trying a new seed cannot separate these two messages.
reader_notes.key: The experiment chooses a 64-bit seed at random, with every possible value equally likely. The two messages are chosen first and do not depend on that seed.
reader_notes.scope: This is an unequal-length collision in mx3 v3’s string-hashing function. It is not a finding about the project’s random-number generator.

rows.name: fasthash-64
rows.label: fasthash-64
rows.scope: Exact sufficient contribution; other pairs or collision events may lower the score. The unversioned fast-hash code is pinned to upstream commit 08a25db2 (2018-10-22). SMHasher3 verification is 0xA16231A7 at 64 bits and 0xE9481AFC at 32 bits. Its wrappers pass a 64-bit seed to both widths; upstream fasthash32 takes a 32-bit seed. The every-seed identity covers both models, which the reproduction program measures separately.
rows.key_model: 64 for fasthash64 (`uint64_t fasthash64(const void *buf, size_t len, uint64_t seed);` fasthash.h line 50); upstream fasthash32 takes `uint32_t seed` (fasthash.h line 42), so nonzero fixed-pair probabilities are at least 2^-32 under a uniform native seed; SMHasher3 passes a 64-bit seed_t to both widths. The seed enters once, `uint64_t h = seed ^ (len * m);` (fasthash.c line 41), before any message word; each 8-byte word (and the zero-padded tail) passes through the public bijection mix() (xorshift 23, *0x2127599bf4325c37, xorshift 47) and then h = (h ^ mix(v)) * m with odd m = 0x880355f21e6d1965; output mix(h).
rows.summary: A seven-byte message and an eight-byte message cancel the hash’s attempt to encode their different lengths. They then follow the same computation for every seed. Reducing the output to 32 bits preserves the collision.

reader_notes.evidence: The algebra shows that this pair collides for every seed. Trying a new seed cannot separate these two messages.
reader_notes.key: The experiment chooses a 64-bit seed at random, with every possible value equally likely. The two messages are chosen first and do not depend on that seed.
reader_notes.scope: Both fasthash32 and fasthash64 are affected by this pair. The appendix gives the bytes and shows how the length difference is cancelled.

rows.name: MuseAir v0.3 (SMHasher3)
rows.label: MuseAir
rows.scope: Exact sufficient contribution; other pairs or collision events may lower the score. SMHasher3 version only. Supplied upstream audit records algorithm v2 / crate 0.6.0 and deprecates earlier versions. Also holds on upstream v0.4; does not transfer to v1/v2 (0/2^24 each). The current v2 has a separate row (32-byte pair, about 19.45 bits).
rows.key_model: Uniform 64-bit seed. Pair collides on both full 128-bit variants and both 64-bit variants.
rows.summary: The v0.3 implementation loses the distinction between two messages before secret mixing. They therefore collide for every seed, giving a 1.59-bit cap. Algorithm v2 has a separate 32-byte witness and a sampled cap of 19.45 bits.

reader_notes.evidence: The every-seed algebraic witness applies to v0.3 and v0.4. It does not transfer to v1 or v2; the separate v2 row uses a different, sampled witness.
reader_notes.key: The experiment chooses a 64-bit seed at random, with every possible value equally likely. The two messages are chosen first and do not depend on that seed.
reader_notes.scope: This 1.59-bit result is version-bound to v0.3 and v0.4. Current algorithm v2 (crate 0.6.0) has its own 19.45-bit sampled result.

rows.name: MuseAir v2 (crate 0.6.0)
rows.label: MuseAir v2
rows.evidence: about 2^-17.45 of keys (sampled; 36,060 events / 1.5×2^32 keys, upstream crate)
rows.scope: Measured score cap with sampling uncertainty; better pairs may exist. Rate quoted for museair::hash with a single uniform 64-bit seed; bfast::hash collides on identical seeds; the 128-bit variants (seed_a, seed_b) collide at the same rate under a two-seed model. Not scored by SMHasher3 (ships v0.3).

rows.summary: A fixed 32-byte change in the tail product can be cancelled by changes in the head when the multiplication carries agree. Upstream crate checks give a sampled cap of 19.45 bits. The v0.3 every-seed witness is a separate result.

reader_notes.evidence: Two fresh upstream-crate runs found 36,060 collisions in 1.5 × 2^32 seeds, about 2^-17.447. The 95% score interval is 19.43–19.46 bits.
reader_notes.key: The scored function draws one uniform 64-bit seed. Both messages are fixed independently of that seed.
reader_notes.scope: This is algorithm v2, crate 0.6.0, timed through a separately validated MuseAir-v2 registration with direct seed mapping. The 64-bit bfast function collides on the same seeds; the 128-bit functions use a separate two-seed model.

rows.name: komihash v5.27 / v5.34
rows.label: komihash
rows.scope: Measured score cap with sampling uncertainty; better pairs may exist. This high-probability construction applies to lengths 64..127 bytes only; not an all-length probability. At 64 bytes (L = 8) no pair can score below 3.00 bits, so this cap is within 0.14 bits of the best possible witness at this length.
rows.key_model: Uniform 64-bit UseSeed.
rows.summary: Two fixed messages that differ in just two bits collide for about 91% of sampled seeds. The parallel calculations are related in a way that lets carefully chosen message changes cancel. A fresh random seed will therefore usually leave this particular pair colliding.

reader_notes.evidence: The sample contains 3,910,946,997 collisions in 2³² seeds: about 91.06%. This is a measured rate, not an exact formula for every possible seed.
reader_notes.key: The experiment chooses a 64-bit seed at random, with every possible value equally likely. The two messages are chosen first and do not depend on that seed.
reader_notes.scope: The construction works at lengths from 64 through 127 bytes. The analysis does not extend this rate to longer inputs that go through another processing round.

rows.name: t1ha2_atonce-64 v2.1.4
rows.label: t1ha2_atonce-64
rows.scope: Measured score cap with sampling uncertainty; better pairs may exist (6-digit routes not enumerated). Cross-length 13/16-byte pair. All 701 uniform-seed hits (3 x 2^36) lie inside the class, so the class contribution is the observed rate at this resolution, but it remains a sampled lower bound on eps, not a proof of total equality.
rows.key_model: Uniform 64-bit one-shot API seed.
rows.summary: A 13-byte input and a 16-byte input can reach the same internal state when multiplication carries cancel. An exactly counted seed class and a measured success rate within it give a sampled cap of 29.19 bits. The result permits different message lengths.

reader_notes.evidence: The seed class fixes 24 bits. The upstream verifier found 58,715,203 collisions in 2^30 class samples, giving a class-weighted rate of about 2^-28.19. Fresh uniform-seed runs support the result.
reader_notes.key: The experiment chooses a 64-bit seed at random, with every possible value equally likely. The two messages are chosen first and do not depend on that seed.
reader_notes.scope: This result concerns the t1ha2_atonce 64-bit function. Other t1ha versions and the streaming interface are separate cases.

rows.name: a5hash v5.21, 64-bit
rows.label: a5hash 64-bit
rows.evidence: collides for at least 118 of every 2^45 keys (counted)
rows.scope: Exact sufficient contribution; other pairs or collision events may lower the score. Exact sufficient seed class, not equality for total epsilon. reader_notes.scope: The results apply to the respective 64-bit and 128-bit functions in the studied a5hash version. The appendix gives separate witnesses and derivations.

rows.name: rapidhash v3
rows.label: rapidhash v3
rows.scope: Measured score cap with sampling uncertainty; better pairs may exist. SMHasher3 tests v3. The first-fold flaw persists in standard, -micro and -nano: each has 11/2^30 at both 32 B and 48 B. The 28.54-bit plotted cap uses L=4 at 32 B; the 48-byte score is 29.125530882083858. Timings shown are for standard v3. A separate upstream-master protected-mode check found no annihilation collisions in 2^26 seeds, while fold pairs A and D each retained 4/2^28 collisions; see records/fairness-pass/rapid3/. Exact Poisson 95% interval for this witness-derived score: [27.7, 29.5]. The annihilation needs the shipped secret array. rapidhash's public API (rapidhash, rapidhash_withSeed, Micro, Nano) exposes only a 64-bit seed; the maintainer keeps the secrets fixed (issue #10, 2024-12-02) and states that random seeds are not recommended and that most users will use seed 0 (issue #10, 2026-01-11). Users who compile their own secret array (secret.h) are outside this witness.
rows.key_model: Uniform 64-bit API seed (sampled reproducibly with xoshiro256**); fixed default public secret/constants
rows.summary: Flipping every bit in two chosen message words can leave a multiplication’s mixed result unchanged. That produces a fixed pair with more collisions than its output width might suggest. The rate is estimated from samples; the chart is not a ranking of hashes, because search effort was unequal.

reader_notes.evidence: The recorded sample found 11 collisions in 2³⁰ seeds. That small count makes the plotted cap an estimate.
reader_notes.key: The experiment chooses a 64-bit seed at random, with every possible value equally likely. The two messages are chosen first and do not depend on that seed.
reader_notes.scope: The experiment uses rapidhash v3’s standard function and its default public constants. Micro, Nano and other releases are not covered by this measurement.

rows.label: foldhash-fast
rows.scope: Same-type 8-byte byte-string witness; quality and equal-length Vec framing preserve accumulator collisions. Cross-type every-instance collisions are separate and do not change this score.

rows.name: MUM v3
rows.label: MUM v3
rows.scope: Exact multiplication, fixed public constants, default macro configuration of mum.h. The key-free 8-byte pair collides for every seed in both the 8-word and 16-word unroll variants and is unaffected by the November 28, 2025 collision-prevention change (commit 52c7d6c), which only guards the paired-word loop for inputs longer than 8×unroll bytes: re-checked against mum.h at 595c091 (2026-06-02) in the default, MUM_V3, MUM_V1 and MUM_V2 builds, 2^20 seeds each. Only the opt-in MUM_QUALITY build, whose remainder-word term is _mum(word + prime, prime), resists this pair; a short rho search on that term gives it its own every-seed 8-byte pair (4f14c5312ab68a6e / 9bff572f76b22816, seed 0 -> 35186508eed8194a). reader_notes.key: Model A starts with 64 independently random bytes: one word expands the block keys, one independently keys Horner, and six supply the finalizer and integer twist. The alternative paper model uses 39 independent words (312 bytes). The small seed used for benchmarking does not meet either assumption.
reader_notes.scope: The guarantee covers fixed-length and at-most-length messages, including unequal lengths, under the stated key distribution. Horner stride, SIMD width, lazy or eager reduction, streaming chunks and valid thread splits leave the digest unchanged. Bulk timings use 256 KiB messages; M2 is the median of three. Sanity and verification passed, but no complete v3 statistical-suite result or machine-checked implementation proof is claimed.

rows.summary: The proof gives at least 125 bits on this post’s collision score when the key contains 160 independently random bytes. Lean, a proof-checking program, has verified the mathematical construction and its key setup. The guarantee does not cover the smaller seed used in the benchmark or establish that the compiled C implementation is correct.

reader_notes.evidence: The checked proof includes empty messages and messages whose length is not a multiple of a machine word. The exact length-dependent probability formula is in the linked specification.
reader_notes.key: Choose twenty independent random 64-bit words, totaling 160 bytes. The theorem covers how the algorithm derives further values from them. The specification calls that setup “model A”; an arbitrary 64-bit seed expander is not equivalent.
